title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 16
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Deforestation in the Amazon Basin
passages.text:
The Amazon rainforest spans approximately 5.5 million square kilometres across nine countries, with Brazil containing about 60 percent of this vast ecosystem. Since the 1970s, deforestation rates have accelerated dramatically, driven by cattle ranching, agricultural expansion, logging, and infrastructure development. Current satellite data indicates that roughly 17 percent of the original forest cover has been lost, pushing the Amazon toward a critical ecological tipping point beyond which it may transform from a carbon sink into a carbon source. This transformation would represent a catastrophic feedback loop, fundamentally altering global climate patterns and eliminating one of Earth's most biodiverse regions.

Deforestation operates through interconnected mechanisms that intensify environmental degradation. Initial clearing typically occurs through logging roads that penetrate pristine forest, fragmenting habitats and facilitating further encroachment. Large-scale cattle operations then replace cleared forest, accounting for approximately 80 percent of deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon. Agricultural frontiers—particularly for soybean cultivation—advance relentlessly northward and westward, consuming previously protected areas. These land-use changes have cascading hydrological effects: reduced evapotranspiration diminishes atmospheric moisture recycling, potentially altering precipitation patterns across South America and beyond. The region's water cycle, which influences rainfall throughout the southern hemisphere, becomes destabilized by expanding deforestation across the basin.

The biodiversity consequences of Amazon deforestation are staggering. The rainforest harbours roughly 10 percent of all known species on Earth, with millions of organisms still undescribed by science. Forest fragmentation isolates animal populations, reducing genetic diversity and increasing extinction risk. Studies suggest that if deforestation exceeds 20–25 percent, the ecosystem may lose its self-regulating capacity, triggering runaway degradation. Indigenous communities and traditional forest peoples have inhabited and sustainably managed these ecosystems for millennia, but modern pressures have displaced hundreds of thousands, destroying irreplaceable cultural knowledge alongside biodiversity. These indigenous groups possess invaluable knowledge of forest resources, sustainable harvesting practices, and medicinal plants that remain incompletely documented by Western science.

Climate implications of Amazon deforestation extend globally. The intact forest stores approximately 150–200 billion tonnes of carbon in its biomass and soil. Deforestation releases this carbon dioxide, while simultaneously eliminating the forest's capacity to absorb future atmospheric CO2. Research suggests Amazon deforestation contributes roughly 5 percent of annual global greenhouse gas emissions—a substantial proportion for a single ecosystem. Regional climate models indicate that continued forest loss could trigger positive feedback loops, reducing rainfall sufficiently to cause transition to savanna-like vegetation in parts of the eastern and southern Amazon within decades.

Governmental and international responses have intensified in recent years. Brazil's Amazon Fund, established in 2008, finances conservation initiatives through international contributions. Protected areas now cover approximately 50 percent of the Brazilian Amazon, though enforcement remains inconsistent. The Paris Climate Agreement has elevated deforestation into global climate negotiations, making forest conservation a central component of climate mitigation strategies. However, political pressures, economic incentives favouring land conversion, and limited funding for effective enforcement continue to challenge conservation efforts. Balancing development aspirations with conservation imperatives remains the central challenge facing Amazonian governance.

passages.title: The Development of the Internet
passages.text:
The internet emerged from military research during the Cold War, specifically from the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), which sought to develop a decentralized communication network resistant to nuclear attack. In 1969, ARPA funded ARPAnet, the first operational packet-switching network, connecting computers at four American universities: UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, University of California at Santa Barbara, and University of Utah. This pioneering network demonstrated that digital information could be reliably transmitted across geographic distances through independently routed data packets.

The development of standardized protocols proved essential for expanding network connectivity. In the 1970s, Robert Kahn and Vint Cerf developed the Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol (TCP/IP), which became the foundational standards enabling diverse computer networks to interconnect seamlessly. TCP/IP's elegant design allowed networks using different hardware and software to communicate through a common interface, facilitating unprecedented interoperability. By 1983, TCP/IP replaced earlier communication protocols as the ARPAnet standard, marking the technical birth of what would become the modern internet. Universities and research institutions rapidly adopted these protocols, creating a growing ecosystem of interconnected networks.

The World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN (European Organization for Nuclear Research) in 1989, transformed the internet from a technical tool into a mass-market phenomenon. Berners-Lee developed three fundamental technologies: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) for document transmission, HTML (HyperText Markup Language) for document formatting, and URLs (Uniform Resource Locators) for resource identification. He crucially released these technologies into the public domain rather than patenting them, enabling rapid global adoption. Early graphical web browsers, particularly Mosaic (released in 1993) and Netscape Navigator, made web navigation intuitive for non-technical users, democratizing internet access across diverse populations.

Commercial expansion in the 1990s transformed the internet's trajectory. The National Science Foundation lifted restrictions on commercial internet use in 1991, triggering an explosion of private companies competing to provide internet services and develop web-based businesses. The dot-com era (1995–2000) saw extraordinary investment in internet startups, many with unsustainable business models. The subsequent market crash eliminated many companies but established surviving firms like Amazon and eBay as dominant platforms. Simultaneously, broadband technologies—particularly cable modems and digital subscriber lines—increased access speeds and bandwidth, enabling multimedia content and real-time services that earlier dial-up connections could not support.

The modern internet has become deeply integrated into global commerce, communication, and information exchange. Mobile broadband expansion from the 2000s onward, driven by smartphones and 4G networks, extended internet access to billions worldwide. Cloud computing, social media platforms, and streaming services now constitute major economic sectors. Simultaneously, emerging concerns about cybersecurity, data privacy, content moderation, and digital inequality challenge internet governance. The internet's evolution from a specialized research tool to an indispensable global infrastructure demonstrates how technological innovation, when made openly accessible, can fundamentally reshape human society within a single generation.
